The African golden cat (Profelis aurata) exhibits a reproductive strategy that includes a gestation period of 81 days [tg = 81 days] when maintained at the species' typical active body temperature of 39.8 °C [T = 39.8 °C]. This duration is somewhat longer than the 75 to 78 day range reported in some earlier compilations, possibly reflecting variation in maternal condition or the thermal environment of the den. Following parturition, the altricial cubs weigh approximately 248.33 grams [Wwb = approximately 248.33 grams] at birth, a value that falls within the broader spectrum of reported neonatal masses for the species, which range from 180 to 235 grams. This initial body mass, though modest relative to the ultimate adult size, reflects the substantial gestational investment required to produce a well-developed foetus capable of surviving the initial weeks of life. The newborn, entirely dependent on its mother, enters a period of intensive parental care that will shape its subsequent developmental trajectory.

During the suckling juvenile stage, the cubs remain entirely reliant on their mother's milk, a period that culminates in weaning. Observations suggest that weaning occurs at 42 days [tx = 42 days] after birth when the mother is at a body temperature of 39.8 °C [T = 39.8 °C], which is the typical core temperature for the species during active periods. This marks the nutritional independence of the kitten and the transition to a diet of solid food, primarily small mammals and birds brought to the den by the mother. The period of complete dependency is relatively brief for a felid of this size, allowing the female to invest in a new litter within the same season if conditions are favorable. The growth rate during this nursing phase is rapid, with cubs gaining mass steadily as they prepare for the challenges of independent hunting and territorial establishment.

The developmental trajectory diverges between the sexes, with notable differences in the timing of reproductive maturation. Under the thermal conditions characteristic of the species' active metabolic state, which is approximately 39.8 °C [T = 39.8 °C], female African golden cats reach puberty at a mean age of 335.5 days [tp = 335.5 days] since birth, whereas males achieve sexual maturity considerably earlier, at around 183 days [tp = around 183 days] since birth. This pronounced sexual dimorphism in maturation timing is a relatively uncommon pattern among solitary felids and may be linked to the species' territorial social structure, where males must disperse and establish home ranges before competing for access to females. The earlier male puberty allows young males to begin scent-marking and patrolling their territories well before they are physically capable of successfully competing with larger, established adult males.

The maximum lifespan recorded for the African golden cat, when measured at a body temperature of 39.8 °C [T = 39.8 °C], is 21 years [am = 21 years], a longevity that is consistent with that of other medium-sized felids inhabiting tropical forests. This extended lifespan, which likely exceeds the typical duration for many smaller carnivores, is believed to be an adaptation to the relatively stable but resource-limited environment of the Central African rainforest. The slow pace of life is further reflected in the species' low reproductive output. Information from field studies indicates that females typically produce a single litter per year [F_R_i = single litter per year], each containing approximately 3 kittens [N_R_i = each containing approximately 3 kittens]. This conservative life-history strategy, prioritizing adult survival over high fecundity, is a common feature of solitary forest-dwelling carnivores.

Females of the species achieve an ultimate wet weight of approximately 10650 grams [Wwi = approximately 10650 grams], representing the asymptotic body mass typically recorded in healthy adult individuals. This value places the species within the lower to middle range of the 5.5 to 16 kilogram body mass spectrum reported in the literature, with females being notably smaller than males. A maximum longevity of 21 years [am = 21 years] places Profelis aurata among the longer-lived medium-sized felids of the African rainforest, comparable to the African leopard (Panthera pardus) but substantially exceeding the 10–15 year maxima recorded for sympatric viverrids and small carnivores at a temperature of 39.8 °C [T = 39.8 °C]. This combination of a moderate adult mass, a relatively long gestation of 81 days [tg = 81 days], and a low reproductive output, with a single litter per year [F_R_i = single litter per year] and a litter size of approximately 3 kittens [N_R_i = a litter size of approximately 3 kittens], suggests that the African golden cat is a K-selected species at a temperature of 39.8 °C [T = 39.8 °C]. Its population dynamics are likely more sensitive to adult mortality than to fluctuations in juvenile survival, a critical consideration for conservation planning in its fragmented forest habitat.
